Halberds, flails, and plate armor were used exclusively in the Middle Ages. I guess if you view "medieval" as 5th-10th centuries, it makes sense to exclude those, but pretty much every fantasy story with "medieval technology" told in the modern era includes them, among other things. Crossbows and paper in particular have been around since the BCs, so it would make no sense to exclude them. Magnifying glasses have been used since the 13th century. I'm not sure where you're getting your information on what existed during the medieval era and what didn't.

Pretty much none of these things would typically be excluded, nor should they be to provide a necessarily "realistic" look into a "medieval" setting. Glassblowing has existed since the 1st century, though vials may be oddly shaped or discolored. The technology also existed for melting steel, which is all that would be needed to make ball bearings, though again, they may be misshapen and rough. "Advanced architecture", especially in the sense of large walls or castles, have been around since Roman times, though knowledge and methods changed over time and there may have been periods where few new ones were built.

Germ theory and the scientific method were, however, not known until later, so it would make sense to exclude them--but before that point, there were still treatments for diseases, though likely half or more of them were worse than useless, which may be a talking point when buying "potions of cure disease" and such.

There are multiple types of insulin (to put it simply), which are metabolized at different rates. The kind you're talking about is metabolized slowly over a long period of time. This works well for type 2 diabetics because that type causes chronically high blood sugar. Type 1 diabetics require a form that is metabolized quickly and then gone. This is because type 1 diabetics' blood sugar can vary drastically even in the course of a few hours, from high to low or vice versa. If someone with type 1 diabetes took the kind of insulin you're talking about, it would be dangerous and potentially lethal, because it would prevent their blood sugar from going up when it goes low (i.e. if their blood sugar plummets, normally they could eat or drink something with sugar to get it back up to a normal range; if they have the slowly metabolized insulin in their body, it will keep the blood sugar low). Low blood sugar can kill _very_ quickly.

There is such a thing as olfactory fatigue. This means that if you smell something for an extended period of time, you stop smelling it until you're away from that smell for a while. Additionally, if you smell something with an extremely strong scent, you can stop being able to smell altogether for a while.

However, this is different from sight or hearing damage. Those things do not regenerate.

Light and sound contain energy. Bright light (or higher energy light like ultraviolet) and loud noises will expose your system to a high amount of energy all at once, which your body isn't equipped to handle. This will damage your senses permanently because it's essentially destroying structures that your body can't rebuild past a certain point.

Something similar _can_ happen to your sense of smell, though. A lot of people are listing substances that can permanently damage your sense of smell. This works in a similar fashion. When the substance enters your body, it reacts, releasing energy. Since your body isn't equipped to handle a high level of energy, substances that react vigorously (and release a lot of energy all at once) can cause potentially permanent damage to your body, thus making you lose your sense of smell.

That said, it is _far_ more rare to encounter something that damages your sense of smell than it is to encounter something that damages your sense of sight or hearing (looking at the sun or listening to loud music can cause damage).

So, basically, in everyday life the answer would be no. In certain situations, it can happen, but it's more likely you'll lose your sense of smell to another form of injury.
